  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster
  growth and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on an/each Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up to 24 hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov or by completing an online
form at www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Robert Aguirre, Director of Recreation & Community Services
 SUBJECT:  Adopt a resolution dissolving the Sister Cities Commission and adding
  the responsibilities to the Community Participation Commission

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a resolution dissolving the Sister Cities Commission and adding the
  responsibilities previously administered by the Sister Cities Commission to the
  Community Participation Commission; and
  2. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On October 2, 2024, staff provided a report summarizing the activities and status of the
Sister Cities Commission Ad Hoc Committee to the City Council to receive and file.
The Council requested that City staff return to a future meeting with a recommendation
for addressing any pertinent responsibilities of the Sister Cities Commission.

City staff is recommending that the Sister Cities Commission be dissolved due to the
concerns that have been raised by the Ad Hoc Committee. The individual Sister City
Associations may choose to continue operating independently.

The Council can provide direction to add the duties previously administered by the Sister
Cities Commission to the Community Participation Commission. These duties include
participating in the exchange of cultures, participating in the City of Monterey Park’s
cultural events and programs, and serving as cultural ambassadors to sister city visitors.

The Community Participation Commission consists of ten adult members and seven
youth members who meet monthly to discuss and promote youth and community
activities, many of which are cultural in nature. The addition of cultural exchange is in line
with the goals of the Community Participation Commission and will be reflected in a
Resolution amending Section 5(c) of Resolution No. 11589.

BACKGROUND:
On January 17, 2024, staff requested direction from the City Council regarding the Sister
Cities Commission due to concerns with its structure and limitations on oversight.
Subsequently, the City Council suspended the Commission's operations and formed an

ad hoc committee to meet with the five individual Sister City Associations with
representatives on the Commission.

Since its formation in January 2024, the ad hoc committee met on three occasions:
February 13, May 14, and July 30. During the first two committee meetings, the Sister
City Associations decided to independently pursue establishing separate non-profit IRC
501(c)3 organization status for their respective Sister City Associations. During the July
30 meeting of the ad-hoc committee, the Sister City Associations from China and Korea
shared that they were each continuing to work toward establishing their own independent
IRC 501(c)3 organizations but were having difficulty recruiting a sufficient number of
members.

A fourth meeting was scheduled for September 24, 2024. On September 23, the
Quanzhou, China Sister City Association representatives notified City staff that they
would not be attending the meeting and were suspending all operations until an
undetermined date. On the morning of September 24, the representative from New Taipei
City, Taiwan emailed staff to share that they would not be attending the meeting and
asked to be removed from future communication. No representatives from Morelia,
Mexico or Yeongdeungpo-Gu, Korea attended the meeting.

The only Sister City Association with active IRC 501(c)3 status is Nachikatsurra, Japan.

FISCAL IMPACT:
No fiscal impact.

 FROM:  Shawn Igoe, Director of Public Works
 SUBJECT:  Spirit Bus Pilot Program

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute an Amendment with First Transit, in a
  form approved by the City Attorney, for fixed-route transit services for an annual
  amount not-to-exceed $2,064,537 for services through December 31, 2025, with
  the option to continue service on a month-to-month basis; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

BOARD/COMMISSION REVIEW:
The proposed changes were shared with the Traffic Commission on August 22, 2024 and
with the Environmental Commission on August 28, 2024. Both Commissions had positive
feedback regarding the proposed changes to the Spirit Bus program.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City worked with Arcadis/IBI Consultants, Inc (Arcadis-IBI) to complete an evaluation
of its Spirit Bus fixed-route transportation program. As a result of the evaluation, staff
provided service recommendations to City Council on June 18, 2024 and requested City
Council direction on the implementation of a pilot program for the proposed restructure of
routes and implementation of on-demand services. City Council was supportive of the
pilot program and requested staff conduct additional outreach regarding proposed
changes prior to deploying a pilot program. At the November 6, 2024 meeting, City
Council approved on-demand services as part of a one-year pilot program. At this time,
staff recommends City Council authorize an extension to the agreement with First Transit
to continue fixed-route service through the end of the pilot program.

BACKGROUND:
On June 18, 2024, staff provided City Council results of the Spirit Bus evaluation
completed by Arcadis-IBI, including recommended service improvement strategies. The
service improvement strategies include changes to the fixed-route service and
implementation of on-demand zones for microtransit services through a pilot program. A
follow-up online community survey was released to gain feedback on the proposed
program changes. The survey was introduced at the City’s Business Expo event held on

  Page 13 of 389
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 4
November 20, 2024
August 8th, and distributed to local school districts, shared through social media,
Cascades, City website, posted at City facilities and Spirit buses.

There were 174 survey respondents, 70% were current Spirit Bus riders. When asked
how proposed service improvements would affect their travel experience, 50 out of 65
thought it may make it worse. However, several of those respondents indicated they do
not use the primarily affected routes 3 and 4. When asked if the proposed changes would
make them more or less likely to ride Spirit Bus, 85% indicated more likely (71%) or no
change (14%).

Fixed-route Service
The Spirit Bus service operates five local routes and the LINK shuttle service on
weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to approximately 6:30 p.m. Routes 1 to 4 are loop alignments
that link various residential neighborhoods (Brightwood, Highlands, Garvey Ranch) to
commercial areas. Route 5 provides service between Atlantic Square/East Los Angeles
College (ELAC) and the Metrolink commuter rail station at Cal State Los Angeles
(CSULA). The LINK operates as a shuttle service between the LA Corporate Center and
the CSULA Metrolink Station.

As a result of community feedback received through survey research and community
engagement and analysis of existing Spirit Bus services, key service improvement
strategies are recommended to restructure existing routes for enhanced public
transportation program. The recommended route restructuring, as listed below, intends
to reflect a more linear configuration and better connectivity to major trip
attractors/generators while complementing use of microtransit service for single-family
residential neighborhoods that have low fixed-route ridership.

  •  Route 1: Change from one-way loop to linear bi-direction route along Atlantic Blvd.
  Change is directional only, there is no change to area covered or scheduled stops.
  •  Route 2: Change from one-way loop to linear bi-direction route along Garfield Ave.
  Change is directional only, there is no change to area covered or scheduled stops.
  •  Route 3: Eliminate service south of Graves to Garvey Ranch and extend route east
  to Atlantic Blvd.
  •  Route 4: Eliminate route and provide coverage to service area through on-demand
  service.
  •  Route 5: Expand service to connect with Metro E Line Station at Atlantic and
  Pomona and eliminate service east of Atlantic and Riggin. Provide additional
  coverage through on-demand service along Riggin Road, including service to the
  Monterey Park Marketplace Shopping Center.

A few respondents from the follow-up survey expressed concern about how the proposed
changes to fixed routes would impact students, specifically those attending Mark Keppel
High School and Brightwood Elementary School. With the proposed changes, Route 1
would continue to provide coverage for service to Mark Keppel High School. Brightwood
Elementary would be served by on-demand microtransit service providing for direct, curb-
to-curb service, thereby limiting the distance students may have to walk to catch a bus.

Additionally, transfers between fixed-route and on-demand microtransit service would
also be available for all bus customers in the Spirit Bus service area.

Staff has been in discussions with First Transit—the City’s current Spirit Bus operator for
the proposed restructuring of routes. To proceed with the changes, the City will need to
extend its current agreement with First Transit for services through the end of the
proposed one-year pilot program. Currently, the term of the agreement with First Transit
is through December 31, 2024, with the option to continue service on a month-to-month
basis until June 30, 2025. It is recommended that the term be extended through
December 31, 2025, and continue on a month-to-month basis.

On November 6, 2024, City Council approved implementation of on-demand services as
part of a one-year pilot program that includes route changes and microtransit services.
While the pilot program is running, staff will collect key data to help develop an RFP for
soliciting fixed-route and/or microtransit services for the community at the conclusion of
the pilot.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The proposed Spirit Bus changes support the City’s strategic goal to maintain fiscal
stability of our City’s financial resources. Results of the Arcadis-IBI’s evaluation identified
service improvements that would maximize the use of City’s financial resources when
providing public transportation. The proposed pilot program would not only provide
expanded coverage for service areas but would replace route segments that are not cost
effective due to low ridership. Additionally, the change in services would improve the
system’s efficiency and offer sustainable public transportation options.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The FY 2024-25 budget includes $2,064,537 for fixed route services. The updated cost
for the restructured Spirit Bus service is $1,738,560 per year. There are sufficient funds
in the FY 24-25 budget for the fixed-route services from First Transit. Costs for FY 2025-
26 services will be budgeted as part of the annual budget process.

  Existing Conditions – Key Design Issues

  1. Routes 1-4 are designed primarily to connect residential neighborhoods to Downtown Monterey
  Park.
  •  Impedes productivity by discouraging two-way passenger traffic across the service day.
  Limited demand for AM travel away from Downtown and PM travel toward Downtown.
  •  Excessive circuity in Downtown area alignments.

  2. Need to simplify or redesign Routes 1 and 2 presently operating one-way loops in opposite
  directions on similar alignments to create bi-directional service to customers.
  •  Confusing to customers because the routes are not the same and so travel times are not
  the same in opposite directions.
  •  Route 2 loop through the Monterey Highlands is a significant inconvenience to most
  customers using the route.
  3. Route 4 should be modified to address Metro’s discontinuation of Route 258 service on
  Monterey Pass Road.
  4. Only Route 5 connects directly to the CSULA Metrolink and Metro J (Silver) Line stations.
  •  Most residents (except Riggin Street) need a two-seat bus ride (i.e., transfer between
  Spirit routes) to travel from residence to the stations.
  5. Spirit’s main transfer point at City Hall for Routes 1-4 is not served by regional bus lines.
  •  Discourages transfers between Spirit and Metro/MBL buses.
  •  Location adds travel time for transferring customers.
  6. Spirit does not connect directly to the E (Gold) Line terminal station on 3rd Street west of Atlantic

Recommended Service Improvement Strategies
Based on the design issues noted above, the technical team presents recommended service
improvement strategies (illustrated in Exhibit 2).
Recommendations:
  i.  Routes 1 and 2 – Restructure for bi-directional travel.
  ii.  Route 3 – Restructure by eliminating service south of Graves to Garvey Ranch (to be
  replaced by on-demand service) and extending route east to Atlantic Blvd.
  iii.  Route 4 – Discontinue and provide coverage to service area through on-demand service.
  iv.  Route 5 - Restructure to expand service to connect with Metro E Line Station at Atlantic
  and Pomona and provide additional coverage through on-demand service along Riggin
  Road, including service to the Monterey Park Marketplace Shopping Center.
  v.  On-Demand Microtransit Pilot Program – 2 zones.

The recommended service improvement strategies are designed to improve service by replacing
poorly performing, infrequent, and circuitous routes with more flexible service that still meets the
needs of residents that live in areas that are not well suited to fixed route transit. It would also
provide a new connection for residents to regional transit and to an important commercial destination
and improve service frequency for Route 3 while adding service through a relatively densely
populated neighborhood.
These improvement strategies were further informed by the following:
  •  Review of pre-pandemic ridership data and a comparison to ridership data gathered since all
  5 Spirit Bus routes resumed service in July 2023.
  •  Review of service cost increases and ridership/revenue decreases
  •  Community outreach and feedback gathered initially in 2022 and updated through additional
  survey research in August 2024.

Recommendation: Implement a one-year pilot program to provide a proof of concept (PoC) of on-

On-Demand Microtransit Pilot Zones

The City has undertaken preliminary discussions with Via Transportation
(provider of advanced public mobility solutions - software and operations for
flexible public transit) for the deployment of the recommended pilot program. Key characteristics
from Via’s proposal for the pilot include:
  •  Via’s app allows for trips to be scheduled via phone; the app also integrates with regional
  transportation for trip planning.
  •  Service options for pick up and drop off areas are based on City’s policy decision. Via
  recommends doing pick up/drop off within a zone to/from a zone.
  •  Wait times with the proposed model of 2 vehicles is a not-to-exceed 15 minutes.
  •  Via requires a one-year commitment for the pilot.
  •  Implementation for the pilot is approximately 12 weeks.
  •  City may consider piggybacking off Via’s King County or City of West Covina contracts.
The latter point is based on Via having provided a copy of their contracts with King County Metro
and the City of West Covina. While either of these contracts would need to be tailored to the

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a resolution approving the Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule
  (ROPS 25-26 A&B) for the period between July 1, 2025 – June 30, 2026;
  2. Approving the Successor Agency Administrative Budget for July 1, 2025 – June
  30, 2026;
  3. Directing staff to post and transmit the ROPS and Administrative Budget to the
  appropriate public agencies; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Existing law requires the Monterey Park Successor Agency (SA) to formulate Recognized
Obligation Payment Schedules (ROPS) under which the SA makes payments for eligible
obligations of the former Redevelopment Agency. The ROPS are considered by the
Successor Agency Board, proposed to the Oversight Board (OB) and, if approved by the
OB, provided to the California Department of Finance for review.

The ROPS is required to be prepared for an entire 12 months. Staff requests that the City
Council, acting on behalf of the SA for the former Monterey Park Redevelopment Agency,
consider and adopt the ROPS 25-26 A&B and the related administrative budget for the
period covering July 1, 2025 – June 30, 2026.

BACKGROUND:
ROPS 25-26 A&B has no new line items and requests an amount of $2,294,510 including
an administrative budget of $190,000 for the period of July 1, 2025 through June 30,
2026.

To meet the deadlines for disbursement of funds from the County of Los Angeles, both
the SA and the OB must approve the ROPS and submit it to the Department of Finance
by January 31, 2025.

prevention and protection capabilities to prevent, response to, and recover from threats
or acts of terrorism.” Monterey Park Fire Department has been awarded SHSP grants in
the past and seeks City Council approval of the SHSP 2023 Grant and subrecipient
agreement.

Security Program. This award has been budgeted in the Fiscal Year 2024-25 budget.

  AN ORDINANCE AMENDING MONTEREY PARK MUNICIPAL CODE
  CHAPTER 21.14 (ZCA-24-02) TO AMEND REGULATIONS GOVERNING
  DATA PROCESSING FACILITIES IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 3(A)

  NOVEMBER 3, 2020).

  The City Council of the City of Monterey Park does ordain as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds and declares that:

  A.  This Ordinance is adopted pursuant to the voters’ directives in Ordinance No.
  2198, as adopted November 3, 2020 via Measure JJ.

  B.  Based upon recommendations of the Saturn Park Advisory Review
  Commission (“SPARC”), the City Council will be considering expansion of
  uses within Saturn Park.

  C.  As a preliminary matter, however, the City Council finds that there is a current
  interest by developers to construct “data centers” within Saturn Park. A
  review of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) confirms that the
  “data center” land use is not considered as part of the current zoning
  regulations. While a “data processing facility” is listed as an allowed land use
  within Saturn Park, that term is not defined. Additionally, since this term was
  added to the MPMC in 1998, it was well before the concept internet
  commerce emerged as the “new economy”; the term did not encompass the
  scope of uses contemplated by contemporary data center developers.

  D.  It is plain that data centers – as they have developed in the 25 years since
  the Saturn Park regulations were first added to the MPMC – are energy
  hungry land uses that are generally aesthetically displeasing and provide few
  public benefits. Current data show that, overall, buildings consume 74% of all
  electricity in the United States.

  E.  Goal 2 of the City’s Environmental Justice Element provides that “Community
  health and the reduction of exposure to environmental pollutants is a priority
  and part of all planning and policy practices.” Additionally, Goal 3.1 provides
  that the City should “[m]aximize the use of the City’s existing open space
  network and recreation facilities by enhancing those facilities and providing
  connections, particularly from disadvantaged neighborhoods.”

  F.  These Goals and Policies reflect the City Council’s overall intent to provide for
  a cleaner, greener, and more enjoyable community both for our current
  residents and for future generations.

  G.  Requiring data centers to adhere with green building principles is a form of
  climate action that minimizes greenhouse gas emissions, relies on energy
  efficiency and renewable resources, conserves water, optimizes material use,

  society.

  H.  Third party rating systems characterize the lifecycle considerations for green
  buildings. These programs can offer credibility, transparency, and
  consistency to project teams in pursuit of an elevated and well-defined
  performance standards for data centers.

  I.  It is in the public interest to update the MPMC as to data centers while also
  considering additional uses for Saturn Park as contemplated by Measure JJ,

EXISTING DATA CENTER REGULATIONS
The current regulations within MPMC Chapter 21.14 were enacted by the voters in 1998
and are generally identified as “Office Professional” or “O-P.” To avoid confusion with
other zoning regulations that were adopted by the City Council in 2013, the regulations
affecting Saturn Park were designated as “O-P (Voter Enacted).”

The City is currently processing an application for a “data center” at 1977 Saturn. One of
the City Council’s topics of discussion – which was also discussed by the SPARC – is the
public interest in regulating data centers within Saturn Park. While the proposed use at
1977 Saturn was classified as a “data processing facility,” voters in 1998 could not have
contemplated a “data center” use.

CURRENT AND PROPOSED DEFINITIONS
The MPMC does not current define a data center; data processing facilities are defined
as

  “a building, dedicated space within a building, or group of buildings primarily
  used for the processing, storage, and management of electronic data on
  less than an acre of land. This type of facility typically involves activities
  such as data entry, storage, conversion, and analysis for onsite use.”

Should the proposed regulations be adopted, the MPMC would be amended to include
the following definition of a “data center”:

  “a building, dedicated space within a building, or group of structures located
  on one or more acres of land used to house a large group of networked
  computer systems used for data storage and processing for off-site users,
  to be used for the remote storage, processing, or distribution of large
  amounts of data. Such facilities may also include air handlers, power
  generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, back-up
  batteries, fire suppression systems, enhanced security features, and other
  associated utility infrastructure to support operations. This definition does
  not apply to smaller data processing facilities that are located on less than
  one acre of land and where such facilities are accessory or incidental to
  another primary use.”

This definition more accurately describes the data centers utilized nationwide for cloud
storage; data transmissions; and other internet related activities. It also reflects the
resource intense nature of such land uses.

PROPOSED REGULATIONS
The proposed regulations would help mitigate the impact of data centers on both
surrounding land uses and on environmental resources. These efforts are reflected in:

  •  Aesthetics – the proposed design guidelines would craft data center buildings that
  are more than a box with wires. Such structures should help enhance the Saturn
  Park community and its surroundings with attractive architectural.

  •  Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (“LEED®”) certified building
  designs for sustainable construction – this will help alleviate the impact of data

  centers on energy, water, and other resources. The intent is to encourage use of

  •  Public benefits – the regulations would require data centers to execute a
  development agreement with the City to ensure that the community benefits from
  the presence of these land uses. Because data centers do not “sell” anything, they
  are not generally a significant source of tax revenue (other than limited property
  taxes). A development agreement will help not only protect the investment of data
  center developers but also provide a vehicle by which benefits may flow to the City.

  •  Green technology – among other things, data center would be required to provide
  onsite electric vehicle charging stations. Additionally, such uses must ensure that
  noise emanating from generators, etc., are reduced to the extent practicable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Water Division is requesting approval of the First Amendment to the Professional
Services Agreements with three laboratory firms – Eurofins, Weck, and Clinical Lab – for
water analyses services. The amendment will increase the combined not to exceed total
from $400,000 to $500,000 annually and extend the term of the agreements to June 30,
2028.

BACKGROUND:
On April 20, 2022, City Council awarded three-year agreements to three labs - Eurofins
Eaton Analytica, LLC, Weck Analytical Environmental Services, Inc. and Clinical Lab of
San Bernardino, Inc. – for water analyses services for a combined total not to exceed
$400,000 annually. These agreements will terminate in May 2025.

Each of the three labs provides specialized services for water production: Weck provides
water sampling analysis for the Water Division’s National Pollutant Discharge Elimination
System (“NPDES”) permit; Clinical provides sampling for the distribution system and the
at well heads (Wells 5, 12, 15 and Wells 1, 3, 10, and Fern); and Eurofins provides
sampling for the Centralized Groundwater Treatment System (“CGTS”).

These labs require certification from the State Division of Drinking Water (“DDW”) to test

The Water Division has established good working relationships with all three labs:

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The City is considering the installation of two drywells for the treatment of stormwater at
different locations within the City. The first location is on New Avenue, North of Graves
Avenue. The second location is near City Hall on Newmark Avenue.

The Public Works Director solicited and obtained two proposals from two geotechnical
firms, Converse Consultants and Terracon to complete geotechnical testing in
preparation for the proposed work. It is recommended that City Council authorize the City
Manager to execute a professional service agreement with Converse Consultants, for the
performance of percolation testing at two locations in the amount of $75,995.

BACKGROUND
Cities that drain to the Rio Hondo, including Monterey Park, must comply with the dry
weather bacteria Total Maximum Daily Load (“TMDL”) for the Rio Hondo. Compliance
means that dry weather flows from these cities cannot contribute to high levels of bacteria
in the Rio Hondo. The City is considering the installation of a drywell to intercept the dry
weather flows to the Rio Hondo prior to its discharge out of the City limits, then directing

The Public Works Director solicited proposals from two geotechnical firms to perform the

  SCOPE OF SERVICES
The objective of the subsurface exploration and percolation testing will be to evaluate the
suitability of the subgrade soil and obtain samples for laboratory testing. Converse will
provide the necessary personnel, equipment and materials to explore the site. Our scope
of work will include the following tasks:

Task 1: Project Set-Up
As part of project set-up, personnel from our office will conduct the following:

    Coordinate site access with the City of Monterey Park.
    Stake/Mark the drilling locations in the field so the drill rig has access to the
  designated locations.
    Notify Underground Service Alert (USA) at least 48 hours prior to drilling to clear
  the drilling locations of any conflict with existing underground utilities.

Task 2: Subsurface Exploration
The purpose of the fieldwork will be to determine the underground conditions and obtain
bulk and undisturbed samples of soil for laboratory testing. Each field investigation
method is presented as follows:

Soil Borings
The purpose of the field investigation is to:

    Obtain subsurface information at the site.
    Obtain undisturbed and bulk samples of the various soils encountered at each
  location for laboratory testing.
    Determine the excavatability of the earth materials.

Based upon our research, the historic highest groundwater level in the area has been
interpreted to be below 100 feet as per the Seismic Hazard Zone Report for the Los
Angeles 7.5 minute Quadrangle, Los Angeles County, California, dated 1998. Based
upon an initial review of near surface soils and groundwater levels nearby.

Task 3: Percolation Testing
A percolation test will be performed at each boring location by using the “Large Diameter
Boring Infiltration Test” method according to GS200.1

At each LID location, an 18-inch diameter auger boring will be drilled to the depth
determined according to the results of the subsurface exploration, Converse currently
assumes those depths will be 30 feet and 50 feet bgs. After boring, two (2) four (4) inch
diameter PVC pipes will be installed, one pipe will be solid from ground surface to
approximately 10 feet below top of the proposed percolation zone, and perforated for the
remainder of the pipe, the other pipe will be perforated to the full depth. The partially solid
pipe will be the water introduction pipe, and the fully perforated pipe will be the water level
measuring pipe.

The remaining void space will be filled with pea-gravel to approximately 1-3 feet below
ground surface

Pre-Soaking
Pre-soaking will be done by inundating the borehole with water through the water
introduction pipe for at least one hour. During pre-soak, the water level will be measured
to ensure that the borehole is being pre-soaked to at least the elevation of the infiltration
zone, or to the maximum output of the water source.

Test Procedure
After presoak, Converse will determine if the test should be a constant or falling head test.
Water level will be monitored as the borehole percolates.

    If water drains in 30 minutes or less, Converse will perform a constant head test.
    If water drains in more than 30 minutes, Converse will perform a falling head test.

Falling Head Test Procedure
After completion of presoak, the borehole shall be inundated with water to a level less
than or equal to the presoak depth via the water introduction pipe. For each successive
percolation test reading, the starting water level must be at or near this initial water depth.

A sounder shall be utilized to determine the water level during each test. All
measurements of water level shall be taken to the nearest 1/8-inch increment via the
water level measuring pipe. Measurements of water level shall be taken every half-hour.
Percolation test readings shall be conducted a minimum of six times (for a total of three
hours testing), or when a stabilized rate of drop has been obtained, whichever occurs
first. A stabilized rate is defined as when the highest and lowest readings of water level
drop of three consecutive percolation tests are within 10 percent of each other. The
average of the stabilized rate over the last three consecutive test readings shall be used
as the pre-adjusted percolation rate.

Constant Head Procedure
After conclusion of the pre-soak, water will be added to the boring at a rate determined to
maintain a constant water level at approximately the height of the top of the percolation
zone. If the rate of introduction required is greater than the maximum output of the water
supply, the constant head test will be performed at the maximum output of the water
supply.

Water introduction rate and total volume of introduced water will be determined by use of
a 1.5-inch, inline flow meter. Flow rate, total volume of water introduced and water depth
will be measured every 10 minutes, the constant head test will be conducted for three (3)
hours.

At the end of the three hours of testing, Converse will monitor the water level as the
borehole drains, and will present that information in addition to the constant head test
information.

Test Conclusion
At the conclusion of the percolation testing, attempts will be made to remove the pipes
from the borehole. If attempts fail, the pipe will be abandoned in place and the hole
backfilled with cement slurry or grout.

After completion of the percolation testing, boreholes will be backfilled with cement grout
if it is deeper than ten (10) feet as per Los Angeles County Department of Health
requirements. Boring depths less than ten (10) feet will be backfilled with soil cuttings and
nominally compacted. Boreholes will be patched with cold asphalt where applicable.

Analytical Testing

under chain-of-custody control. All sample analyses will be conducted at a standard
turnaround time. The samples will be analyzed as follows:

    EPA 8260 – VOCs and Oxygenates
    EPA 8270 – SVOCs
    EPA 8082 – PCBs

All excess soil cuttings will be contained in eight (8) drums. The drums will be temporarily
stored on the site away from drainage areas and secured from unauthorized entry until
laboratory analytical results are received. The waste will be profiled for the most cost-
effective disposal or recycling option. For budgeting purposes, we have assumed eight
(8) drums of waste will need to be transported and disposed of as non-hazardous waste.

Converse will be responsible for the preparation of waste manifests, and for arranging for
proper transportation and disposal of the waste. A Client representative will be
responsible for signing the manifests as the Generator. Copies of the manifests will be
provided.

Task 4: Laboratory Testing
Soil samples obtained during exploratory drilling will be tested in the Converse laboratory
to evaluate their physical and engineering properties. Laboratory testing may include, but
will not be limited to:

    In situ moisture content and dry densities (ASTM Standard D2216, and D7263)
    Collapse potential
    Grain size distribution (ASTM D6913)
    Soils corrosivity (Caltrans 643, 422, 417)
    Atterberg limits (ASTM D4318)

Samples will be stored in the Converse laboratory for at least 60 days after the report is
completed. At that time, samples will be disposed of unless we receive notification to do
otherwise.

We will evaluate the data obtained from the exploratory borings and laboratory testing.
We will also conduct engineering analyses in order to present percolation design

40. WATER POLLUTION CONTROL

The following requirements are added to establish storm water and urban runoff pollution
prevention controls.

Storm or construction generated water containing sediment such as, construction waste,
soil, slurry from concrete/asphalt concrete saw cutting operations, clean-up of concrete
transit mixers or other pollutants from construction sites and parking areas will be
retained or controlled on site and will not be permitted to enter the storm drain system.

Temporary sediment filtering systems such as sandbags, silt fences, or gravel berms
will be utilized to trap sediment so that only filtered water enters the City’s storm drain
system. Proper clean up and disposal of settled sediment and the filtering system will be
the responsibility of the Contractor.

Discharge of concrete transit mixer wash water on to approved dirt areas (sub-grade area
designated for new concrete construction for example) is acceptable. Discharge on to
private property, parkway areas, or the street is not permitted.

Plastic or other impervious covering will be installed where appropriate to prevent
erosion of an otherwise unprotected area, along with any other runoff control devices
deemed appropriate by the City.

Excavated soil stored on the site will be covered in a manner that minimizes the amount
of sediments running into the storm drain system, street or adjoining properties.

No washing of construction or other industrial vehicles and equipment will be allowed
adjacent to a construction site. During the rainy season (October 15 to April 15),
Contractor will keep at the construction site sufficient materials and labor to install
temporary sediment filtering systems and other water pollution prevention control

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed Ordinance pursuant to the
California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”)
and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq.,
the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guideline § 15301(c) (Existing Facilities) exempts the
operation, repair, maintenance, alteration of existing public or private structures which
involve negligible or no expansion of existing or former use. The proposed work will occur
entirely within an existing structure. Accordingly, no further environmental review is
required.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Capital Improvement Project (“CIP”) No. 96054 – 2024-25 Concrete Improvement Project
includes curb ramp construction at various street intersections, sidewalk, and curb and
gutter improvements (the “Project”). Pursuant to Resolution No. 2024-R48, the Public
Works Director solicited bids for the 2024-25 Concrete Improvements Project
(Specification No. 2024-005).

The Notice Inviting Bids for this project was published with HLR Media LLC - Monterey
Park Press on September 30 and October 07, 2024 with a bid due date of October 22,
2024. The public bid opening for the 2024-25 Concrete Improvement Project was held on
October 22, 2024. Eight bids were received: NPL Construction Co., Gentry General
Engineering, Onyx Paving Co, Inc., CT&T Concrete Paving, Kalban, Inc, Toro
Enterprises, Inc, Gentry Brothers, Inc., US Builder and Constructions, Inc. It is
recommended that City Council authorize the City Manager to execute a Public Works

BACKGROUND
The Project is in anticipation of the City’s upcoming road rehabilitation project. The Public
Works Director advertised the Project separately as it was determined the City receives
more competitive bids when concrete contractors are the main bidders rather than sub-
contractors when bidding as part of pavement rehabilitation projects.

The Project includes the reconstruction of 70 existing curb ramps in order to meet current
ADA standards, 12,700 s.f. of sidewalk replacement and 100 l.f. of curb and gutter
reconstruction.

The Notice Inviting Bids for this project was published with HLR Media LLC - Monterey
Park Press on September 30 and October 07, 2024 with a bid due date of October 22,
2024. The bid opening for the project was held on October 22, 2024 at 10am, and include
the following bids:

employment of apprentices by the Contractor or any subcontractor.

Labor Code § 1777.5 requires the Contractor or subcontractor employing tradesmen in
any apprenticeship occupation to apply to the joint apprenticeship committee nearest the
site of the public works project and which administers the apprenticeship program in that
trade for a certificate of approval. The certificate will also fix the ratio of apprentices to
journeymen that will be used in the performance of the contract. The ratio of apprentices
to journeymen in such cases will not be less than one to five except:

    When employment in the area of coverage by the joint apprenticeship committee
  has exceeded an average of 15 percent in the 90 calendar days before the
  request for certificate, or

    When the number of apprentices in training in the area exceeds a ratio of one to
  five, or

    When the trade can show that it is replacing at least 1/30 of its membership
  through apprenticeship training on an annual basis state-wide or locally, or

    When the Contractor provides evidence that the Contractor employs registered
  apprentices on all of his contracts on an annual average of not less than one
  apprentice to eight journeymen.

The Contractor is required to make contributions to funds established for the
administration of apprenticeship programs if the Contractor employs registered
apprentices or journeymen in any apprenticeable trade on such contracts and if other
contractors on the public works site are making such contributions.

40. WATER POLLUTION CONTROL

The following requirements are added to establish storm water and urban runoff pollution
prevention controls.

Storm or construction generated water containing sediment such as, construction waste,
soil, slurry from concrete/asphalt concrete saw cutting operations, clean-up of concrete
transit mixers or other pollutants from construction sites and parking areas will be
retained or controlled on site and will not be permitted to enter the storm drain system.

Temporary sediment filtering systems such as sandbags, silt fences, or gravel berms
will be utilized to trap sediment so that only filtered water enters the City’s storm drain
system. Proper clean up and disposal of settled sediment and the filtering system will be
the responsibility of the Contractor.

Discharge of concrete transit mixer wash water on to approved dirt areas (sub-grade area
designated for new concrete construction for example) is acceptable. Discharge on to
private property, parkway areas, or the street is not permitted.

Plastic or other impervious covering will be installed where appropriate to prevent
erosion of an otherwise unprotected area, along with any other runoff control devices
deemed appropriate by the City.

Excavated soil stored on the site will be covered in a manner that minimizes the amount
of sediments running into the storm drain system, street or adjoining properties.

No washing of construction or other industrial vehicles and equipment will be allowed
adjacent to a construction site. During the rainy season (October 15 to April 15),
Contractor will keep at the construction site sufficient materials and labor to install
temporary sediment filtering systems and other water pollution prevention control

The Contractor will notify the occupants of all affected properties at least 48 hours before

to the face of any curb, pole, barricade, delineator, or other vertical obstruction.

One four-foot-wide paved pedestrian walkway will be maintained in the parkway area on
each side of all streets. The clearance from the pedestrian walkway to any traffic lane

   RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION ADOPTED BY THE CITY COUNCIL
  TERMINATING THE REPLACEMENT OF THE HVAC
  SYSTEM AT THE LANGLEY SENIOR CITIZEN
  CENTER LOCAL EMERGENCY

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A.  Pursuant to Resolution No. 2024-R76 (“Emergency Resolution”) the City
  Manager exercised emergency powers replace the HVAC system at the
  Langley Senior Citizen Center.

  B.  Replacement of the HVAC system at the Langley Senor Citizen Center
  (“Project”) is identified as the removal of the existing HVAC unit and
  installation of one Packaged Rooftop Heat Pump Unit curb adapter.

  C.  The circumstances necessitating the declaration of an emergency no longer
  exist and the local emergency is terminated, effective immediately.

SECTION 2: Ratification. The City Council received regular reports regarding the Project
and is fully informed regarding all actions undertaken by the City Manager to protect public
health and safety. Accordingly, the City Council ratifies and reaffirms the exercise of
emergency powers since 2024 to protect public health and safety.

SECTION 3: Termination of Local Emergency. The Replacement of the HVAC System
at the Langley Senior Citizen Center local emergency is terminated.

SECTION 3: Electronic Signatures. This Resolution may be executed with electronic
signatures in accordance with Government Code §16.5. Such electronic signatures will
be treated in all respects as having the same effect as an original signature.

SECTION 4: Recordation. The Mayor, or presiding officer, is authorized to sign this
Resolution signifying its adoption by the City Council of the City of Monterey Park and the
City Clerk, or her duly appointed deputy, may attest thereto.

SECTION 5: Effective Date. This Resolution will become effective immediately upon
adoption and will remain effective unless repealed or superseded.

  PASSED AND ADOPTED this 20th day of November, 2024.

  RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY
  PARK, CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING
  NOVEMBER 30, 2024 AS SMALL BUSINESS SATURDAY

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. Monterey Park celebrates our local small businesses and the contributions they
  make to our local economy and community.

  B. According to the United States Small Business Administration, there are 34.7
  million small businesses in the United States, small businesses represent 99.7%
  of firms with paid employees, small businesses are responsible for 61.1% of net
  new jobs created since 1995, and small businesses employ 45.9% of the
  employees in the private sector in the United States.

  C. Of the approximately 4,700 businesses within the City of Monterey Park, 3,243 or
  70% are considered a small business.

  D. Monterey Park supports local businesses that create jobs, boost the local
  economy, and preserve communities, through innovative programs, streamlined
  processes, and a collaborative approach to economic development. The City’s
  dedication to supporting businesses is shown through initiatives such as the
  Monterey Park Business Connect support program, the Small Business Expo, and
  its proactive business attraction and retention strategies.

  E. On November 6, 2024, the City of Monterey Park won the Los Angeles County
  Economic Development Corporation’s (LAEDC) 2024 Most Business-Friendly City
  Award for small cities for its outstanding efforts in creating a supportive and thriving
  business environment.

  F. Sixty-eight cents of every dollar spent at a small business in the U.S. stays in the
  local community and every dollar spent at small businesses creates an additional
  48 cents in local business activity as a result of employees and local businesses
  purchasing local goods and services.

  G. 59% of U.S. consumers aware of Small Business Saturday shopped or ate at a
  small, independently owned retailer or restaurant on Small Business Saturday
  2023.

  H. Advocacy groups, as well as public and private organizations, across the country
  have endorsed the Saturday after Thanksgiving as Small Business Saturday.

  I. The City Council of Monterey Park does hereby proclaim, November 30, 2024, as
  SMALL BUSINESS SATURDAY

  Page 388 of 389
   J. Furthermore, the City Council urges the residents of our community, and
  communities across the country, to support small businesses and merchants on
  Small Business Saturday – celebrating its 15th year in 2024 – and Shop Small
  throughout the year.

SECTION 2: Electronic Signatures. This Resolution may be executed with electronic
signatures in accordance with Government Code §16.5. Such electronic signatures will
be treated in all respects as having the same effect as an original signature.

SECTION 3: Recordation. The Mayor, or presiding officer, is authorized to sign this

the City Clerk, or her duly appointed deputy, may attest thereto.

SECTION 4: Effective Date. This Resolution will become effective immediately upon
adoption and will remain effective unless repealed or superseded.

  PASSED AND ADOPTED this 20th day of November 2024.

  MINUTES
  MONTEREY PARK CITY COUNCIL
  FINANCING AUTHORITY (MPFA)
  HOUSING AUTHORITY (MPHA)
  GEOLOGIC HAZARD ABATEMENT DISTRICT (GHAD)
  SUCCESSOR AGENCY (SA)
  REGULAR MEETING
  NOVEMBER 20, 2024

The City Council, the Financing Authority (MPFA), the Housing Authority (MPHA), the
Geologic Hazard Abatement District (GHAD), and the Successor Agency (SA) of the City
of Monterey Park held a Regular Meeting of the Council in the Council Chamber, located
at 320 West Newmark Avenue in the City of Monterey Park, Wednesday, November 20,
2024 at 6:30 p.m.

CALL TO ORDER:
Mayor Wong called the meeting to order at 6:38 p.m.

FLAG SALUTE:
The Monterey Park Police Explorers led the flag salute.

ROLL CALL:
City Clerk Maychelle Yee called the roll:

Council Members Present:  Henry Lo, Vinh Ngo, Jose Sanchez, Thomas Wong,
  Yvonne Yiu
Council Members Absent:  None

ALSO PRESENT: City Treasurer Amy Lee, City Manager Inez Alvarez, City Attorney
Karl Berger, Director of Finance Martha Garcia, Fire Chief Chris Thompson, Director of
Human Resources and Risk Management Christine Tomikawa, Director of Community
Development Jessica Serrano, City Librarian Kristin Olivarez, Director of Public Works
Shawn Igoe, Police Chief Scott Wiese, Economic Development Manager Joseph Torres,
Administrative Manager Xochitl Tipan, Financial Services Manager Laura Borjon,
Engineering Manager/Transtech Consultant Ziad Mazboudi, Deputy City Clerk Cindy
Trang

VIRTUALLY PRESENT: None.

AGENDA ADDITIONS, DELETIONS, CHANGES AND ADOPTIONS: None.

  MISSION STATEMENT
 The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth and opportunity,
  and create a joyous and collaborative environment.
  .
   72-296

PUBLIC COMMUNICATIONS

  - Edward Wong from the Wong Tai Sen Taoism Center, shared his appreciation
  to the City Council and to city staff for all their hard work. Dora Leung, President
  of the Monterey Park Chamber of Commerce alongside Reggie Shum, presented
  certificates of appreciation to three departments in the city: the City Manager’s
  Office, the Police Department and the Fire Department. Edward concluded by
  presenting his donation of 350 dinner vouchers for Capital Seafood Restaurant
  to the city staff of Monterey Park.

  - Jessica Alvarenga, Public Affairs Manager for SoCalGas, introduced herself as
  the representative for Monterey Park.

  - Vincent Tsang, representative of Rykadan Capital 005, LLC showed his
  appreciation to the city and submitted physical documentation of their company’s
  progress on the Celadon Mixed-Use/Housing Development Project to the City
  Clerk.

  - City Clerk Yee received, read and filed into the record a written communication
  from Natalie Vega. Natalie questioned what the city’s plans are for creating a
  more diverse shopping selection and spoke about the need for an upgrade to
  drive in more businesses and consumer action.

STAFF COMMUNICATIONS

  - Community Development: Economic Development Manager Torres presented a
  PowerPoint presentation about the positive responses received from the launch
  of the Taste of Downtown Monterey Park program and announced the Monterey
  Park Business Alliance (MPBA), a city led initiative to empower and support local
  businesses.

  - Recreation and Community Services: Director of Recreation and Community
  Services Aguirre provided a PowerPoint presentation about the upcoming events
  in the city which include Letters to Santa, the Holiday Snow Village event and
  Santa’s Jolly Journey.

1.  PRESENTATION
  The matters listed under presentation are informational content and for discussion
  only.

1-A.  WORLD JOURNAL – LUNAR NEW YEAR FESTIVAL UPDATES

  Allan Liu from World Journal LA, LLC provided a progress update on the vendors,
  sponsors and entertainment set to appear at the 2025 Lunar New Year Festival.
   72-297

1-B.  EAST LOS ANGELES COLLEGE – UPDATES

  Vice President of Student Services, Miguel Dueñas, spoke about East Los Angeles
  Community College’s (ELAC) recognition for receiving the 2024 Dr. Rice Award
  for Diversity and Equity and emphasized the need to grow ELAC’s safety among
  the community. Director of the Vincent Price Museum, Steven Wong, depicted in
  detail ELAC’s plan to expand and diversify the accessibility of Art Education among
  the community. Interim Vice President of Administrative Services, Nghi Nghiem,
  provided progress updates on the Kinesiology, Wellness and Athletic Complex
  (KWAC) and introduced Harley Ellis Devereaux (HED) Sector Leader, Martha Ball,
  and HED Architecture Leader, Michael Bulander, to speak on the project. Ball
  spoke about the project’s specifications to cater to the students needs while also
  providing community engagement and Bulander depicted the project’s
  walkthrough experience.

2.  OLD BUSINESS:

2-A.  ADOPT A RESOLUTION DISSOLVING THE SISTER CITIES COMMISSION
  AND  ADDING  THE  RESPONSIBILITIES TO  THE  COMMUNITY
  PARTICIPATION COMMISSION

  On October 2, 2024, staff provided a report summarizing the activities and status
  of the Sister Cities Commission Ad Hoc Committee to the City Council to receive
  and file. The Council requested that City staff return to a future meeting with a
  recommendation for addressing any pertinent responsibilities of the Sister Cities
  Commission.

  City staff is recommending that the Sister Cities Commission be dissolved due to
  the concerns that have been raised by the Ad Hoc Committee. The individual Sister
  City Associations may choose to continue operating independently.

  Action Taken: The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-R91, dissolving the
  Sister Cities Commission and adding the responsibilities previously administered
  by the Sister Cities Commission to the Community Participation Commission.

  Motion: Moved by Council Member Sanchez and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem
  Ngo, motion carried by the following vote:

  Ayes:  Council Members:  Sanchez, Lo, Yiu, Ngo, Wong
  Noes:  Council Members:  None
  Absent:  Council Members:  None
  Abstain:  Council Members:  None
  Recusal:  Council Members:  None
   72-298

  Resolution No. 2024-R91
  A RESOLUTION TRANSFERRING FUNCTIONS FROM THE SISTER CITIES
  COMMISSION TO THE COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION COMMISSION AND
  DISSOLVING THE SISTER CITIES COMMISSION

2-B.  SPIRIT BUS PILOT PROGRAM

  The City worked with Arcadis/IBI Consultants, Inc (Arcadis-IBI) to complete an
  evaluation of its Spirit Bus fixed-route transportation program. As a result of the
  evaluation, staff provided service recommendations to City Council on June 18,
  2024 and requested City Council direction on the implementation of a pilot program
  for the proposed restructure of routes and implementation of on-demand services.
  City Council was supportive of the pilot program and requested staff conduct
  additional outreach regarding proposed changes prior to deploying a pilot program.
  At the November 6, 2024 meeting, City Council approved on-demand services as
  part of a one-year pilot program. At this time, staff recommends City Council
  authorize an extension to the agreement with First Transit to continue fixed-route
  service through the end of the pilot program.

  Public Speakers:

  - Ricardo Martin conveyed his opinion about a potential lack of accessibility for
  children and the elderly utilizing the on-demand service in exchange for
  eliminating Route 4.

  - City Clerk Yee received, read, and filed into the record a written communication
  from Bill Lam. Bill raised concerns about the on-demand services, claiming it may
  be inaccessible to residents that do not own a cell phone and provided different
  route suggestions.

  Discussion: All City Council Members had a Conflict of Interest as their properties
  resides within 500 feet of the proposed project. City Attorney Berger conducted a
  random drawing resulting in Council Member Yiu and Council Member Lo recusing
  themselves from the discussion.

  Administrative Manager Tipan provided a PowerPoint Presentation depicting in
  detail the service improvement strategies for the proposed Spirit Bus route
  changes and the pilot on-demand service to residents.

  Arcadis IBI Associate Steve Wilks was available for questions.

  Existing law requires the Monterey Park Successor Agency (SA) to formulate
  Recognized Obligation Payment Schedules (ROPS) under which the SA makes
  payments for eligible obligations of the former Redevelopment Agency. The ROPS
  are considered by the Successor Agency Board, proposed to the Oversight Board
  (OB) and, if approved by the OB, provided to the California Department of Finance
  for review.

  The ROPS is required to be prepared for an entire 12 months. Staff requests that
  the City Council, acting on behalf of the SA for the former Monterey Park
  Redevelopment Agency, consider and adopt the ROPS 25-26 A&B and the related
  administrative budget for the period covering July 1, 2025 – June 30, 2026.

  Action Taken: The City Council adopted (1) Resolution No. SA-191 approving

  between July 1, 2025 – June 30, 2026; (2) approved the Successor Agency
  Administrative Budget for July 1, 2025 – June 30, 2026; and (3) directed staff to
  post and transmit the ROPS and Administrative Budget to the appropriate public
  agencies, on Consent Calendar.
